paragraphs.heading: What the argument is not
paragraphs.edited: Let's take a minute and flesh this out. When developed, this is referred to as the moral argument for the existence of God. Keep something in mind before we look at the particulars. We're not saying that people have to believe in God to be moral. We're not saying that people have to believe in God to know right from wrong. Atheists can be moral. Pantheists can be moral. Christians can be immoral. But we are arguing that if there is an objective moral standard, then there must be a God.

paragraphs.heading: If there is no God
paragraphs.edited: In his classic novel The Brothers Karamazov, Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky famously said, if there is no God, all is permissible. In other words, if there's not a transcendent moral source outside of human beings, then anything goes. The late atheist philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche said that if there is no God, then it's those with power who get to determine right and wrong. In other words, if God doesn't exist, then it's those with the biggest guns who get to determine morality.

paragraphs.heading: The first premise
paragraphs.edited: So here's the moral argument for the existence of God stated more formally. It has two premises and a conclusion. The first premise is that if there are objective moral values and duties, then God must exist. So what is it about morality that points toward God? For one, moral values and duties aren't physical. You can't weigh them, they don't have extension in space, they can't be studied by science. Moral values and duties contain information, commands about how we are supposed to live. They point toward a source outside of mankind, instructing us about how we're supposed to behave. There's something about moral values and duties that has a spiritual core.

paragraphs.heading: The second premise
paragraphs.edited: The second premise is that objective moral values and duties exist. How can I make such a claim? There are two reasons. For one, in his classic book The Abolition of Man, C.S. Lewis famously pointed out that across cultures throughout the history of the world there's a commitment to certain universal moral principles: that justice is better than injustice, that courage is good, that we ought to care for our children and our posterity. As Lewis points out, how we practice those moral principles might vary across culture, but there is a universal agreement and commitment to the underlying moral principles.

paragraphs.heading: A debate about morality
paragraphs.edited: A few years ago I sponsored a public debate with three of my high school students and three students from the public school free-thinking atheist agnostic club. They debated the historical Jesus, intelligent design, and morality. One of my students got up there and said, there is an objective moral law, we know it, therefore there's a moral law giver. Morality points toward God. Then one of their students got up there and said, there is no objective moral law. In fact, morality is all subjective. It's like picking an ice cream flavor. You have your moral truth and I have mine, and we all live accordingly.

paragraphs.heading: What the argument shows
paragraphs.edited: Simply put, this argument shows that the best explanation for the existence of objective moral values and duties is that there is a personal God. Now, this alone doesn't prove that the Christian God exists. It raises challenges for both pantheism and naturalism, but broadly speaking it's consistent with a God of Judaism and a God of Islam. What this argument shows is that the physical world is not all that exists. There is a spiritual and a moral realm. There is a God who cares about the way that we live. There is a God who will hold us accountable for how we live our lives.
